nameStory: The name 'click beetle' comes from these insects' amazing ability to flip themselves right-side up with an audible 'click' sound when placed on their backs. They arch their bodies and snap a spine-like projection into a groove on their underside, launching themselves several inches into the air with a distinctive clicking noise that delights kids and surprises adults.
description: Monocrepidius lividus is a medium-sized click beetle that's one of New England's more common members of this acrobatic insect family. These oval-shaped beetles typically measure about half an inch long and have a somewhat flattened appearance with a dull brown to blackish coloration. Like all click beetles, they have distinctly segmented antennae and can perform their signature flipping trick when disturbed. Adults are most active during warm evenings and are often attracted to porch lights and windows.

idTips.label: Click mechanism
idTips.description: When flipped onto its back, it will arch its body and snap upward with a loud click sound - try gently placing one upside down to see this amazing behavior

idTips.label: Body shape
idTips.description: Oval and somewhat flattened with parallel sides, feels smooth and hard like a small pebble when handled

idTips.label: Coloration
idTips.description: Dull brownish-black to dark reddish-brown, sometimes with a slightly mottled appearance that can look almost metallic in bright light

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: About 12-15mm long (roughly half an inch), making it one of the larger click beetles you'll encounter in the region

idTips.label: Antennae
idTips.description: Distinctly segmented antennae that look almost saw-toothed or beaded when viewed closely

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: Smooth, hard exoskeleton that feels almost ceramic-like to the touch, with fine punctures visible under magnification

habitat: Found in woodlands, forest edges, and suburban areas with mature trees throughout New England. Adults are commonly encountered around outdoor lights at night, on tree bark, or crawling on the ground near decaying logs. Their larvae live in soil and rotting wood, so adults are often found in areas with rich organic matter and established vegetation.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring as temperatures warm, becoming more active in May and early June. Look for them crawling on tree bark or attracted to porch lights on warm evenings.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity period when adults are most commonly seen. They're frequently attracted to outdoor lighting and can be found on building walls, screens, and around outdoor dining areas on warm summer nights.
seasonality.fall: Activity decreases as temperatures cool, with fewer adults visible by October. Late-season individuals may still be found on unusually warm autumn evenings.
seasonality.winter: Adults overwinter in protected locations under bark, logs, or leaf litter and are rarely seen. Larvae continue developing in soil and decaying wood throughout winter.

funFact: Click beetles can launch themselves up to 25 times their own body length into the air - equivalent to a human jumping over a 30-story building! This incredible feat generates forces of over 400 Gs, which would knock a person unconscious, but the beetle lands perfectly ready to walk away.
confusionNotes: Most easily confused with ground beetles or darkling beetles, but the click mechanism is a dead giveaway - no other beetles can perform this acrobatic flip. If you're unsure, gently place the beetle on its back and see if it clicks and jumps to right itself.
contextualKnowledge: Click beetle larvae are called 'wireworms' and can actually be agricultural pests, feeding on plant roots and seeds. However, the adults are generally beneficial, feeding on other insects and contributing to ecosystem balance.
compareHints: Since this is the only Monocrepidius species commonly found in New England, compare it with other click beetles like Alaus oculatus (the eyed click beetle) which is much larger with distinctive eye spots, or smaller click beetles which are typically under 10mm long. Monocrepidius lividus falls right in the middle size range and lacks the dramatic markings of some relatives.
